title: Beaujolais
description: Granite hills south of Burgundy, where Gamay makes everything from Nouveau to serious crus.
L: Beaujolais lies just south of the Mâconnais, north of Lyon, in eastern France. It has about 13,000 hectares of vines on rolling hills. The climate is semi-continental, warmer than the Côte d'Or. Administratively it belongs to Burgundy, but its grape, soils and style are its own.

Beaujolais divides in two. The north, the Haut-Beaujolais, has pink granite and schist hills, where the best wines grow: Beaujolais-Villages and the ten crus. The south, the Bas-Beaujolais, has clay and limestone, called pierres dorées, golden stones, and makes simpler Beaujolais, including much of the Nouveau.
Where do Beaujolais' best wines grow?
Granite in the north suits Gamay best.

Beaujolais has long been the everyday wine of Lyon, France's food capital, served in its bouchons, traditional bistros, from a pot, a thick-bottomed bottle. The saying goes that Lyon is watered by three rivers: the Rhône, the Saône and the Beaujolais.
Beaujolais' northern hills are mainly granite.
Yes. Pink granite and schist dominate the north.
Beaujolais lies between the Mâconnais and Lyon
Northern granite gives the best wines; the south is limestone

Almost all Beaujolais is Gamay, fully Gamay Noir à Jus Blanc. It gives light to medium-bodied reds with red cherry, raspberry, violet and fresh acidity, and low tannin. Beaujolais has nearly all the world's Gamay. Pruned in gobelet, bush style, on the hills, it suits granite's poor, well-drained soils.

Much Beaujolais uses semi-carbonic maceration. Whole bunches go into a tank; the bottom ones are crushed and ferment, releasing carbon dioxide. The upper berries ferment inside their skins, giving fruity aromas like banana, bubblegum and cherry, with little tannin. Some crus use more traditional methods for structure.
What does semi-carbonic maceration give Beaujolais?
Whole-berry fermentation gives fruity, soft wines.

A small amount of Beaujolais Blanc is made from Chardonnay, mostly in the north, near the Mâconnais. It's fresh and fruity, similar to Mâcon. Rosé is also made from Gamay. But red Gamay is over 95% of production.
Which are features of Gamay in Beaujolais?
Semi-carbonic maceration gives fruity, soft wines
A little Chardonnay makes Beaujolais Blanc

Beaujolais has three main levels. Beaujolais, mostly from the south, light and fruity. Beaujolais-Villages, from 38 villages in the north, with more depth. And the ten crus, named villages on granite, at the top. Crus labels often don't say Beaujolais at all, just the village name.

The ten crus, north to south: Saint-Amour, Juliénas, Chénas, Moulin-à-Vent, Fleurie, Chiroubles, Morgon, Régnié, Brouilly and Côte de Brouilly. Fleurie, Chiroubles and Saint-Amour are light and floral. Morgon, on decomposed schist, and Moulin-à-Vent, on granite with manganese, are the most structured and age well.
Fleurie floral; Morgon and Moulin-à-Vent firm
Match each cru to its style.
The crus range from light to structured.
Aged Morgon and Moulin-à-Vent can taste like Burgundy. Locals say the wine pinote, becomes Pinot-like, with age.
Ten named villages on the northern granite.
Beaujolais has three levels: Beaujolais, Villages, crus
The ten crus range from light Fleurie to firm Moulin-à-Vent
Morgon and Moulin-à-Vent can age like Burgundy
Reading Beaujolais and eating with it

Beaujolais Nouveau is released on the third Thursday of November, weeks after harvest, made quickly by semi-carbonic maceration to be drunk at once. Its success from the 1970s to the 1990s made Beaujolais famous, but also hurt its image for serious wine. Today, crus and natural wine producers, like Marcel Lapierre, have restored its reputation.

Beaujolais is one of the most food-friendly reds: charcuterie, saucisson, roast chicken, pâté, Lyon's bistro dishes, salads, even salmon. Crus suit duck, pork and coq au vin. Serve slightly cool, at 12 to 14 degrees. Nouveau within months; crus from 2 to 10 years.
On a wine list, a cru Beaujolais is often the best-value red. Look for Morgon, Fleurie or Moulin-à-Vent.
Beaujolais is best served slightly cool.
Yes. A slight chill, 12 to 14 degrees, brings out its fruit.

Not true. It's almost all Gamay.
